narrative.title: Why institutional pharma sales, why now
narrative.body:
I spent the first part of my career in institutional finance, most recently at Goldman Sachs, managing 20+ institutional relationships across multi-million dollar syndicated loan portfolios. The real skill there wasn't the transactions. It was learning to navigate accounts where the decision never rested with one person: I had to earn trust across multiple stakeholders with different priorities and get them aligned before anything moved forward. In 2023, I stepped back to raise my two kids.

In 2025, I watched a stranger save someone's life during a medical emergency, and it pushed me to earn my EMT license. I finished in the top 5% of my cohort at UT Dallas, working inside a hospital system across the emergency department, patient transfers, and ambulance care, and completing training in pharmacology fundamentals. What stayed with me was how often a patient's outcome traced back to whether the right treatment reached them in time, and whether everyone around that patient, from the ER physician to the receiving team, had the right information to act fast. In stroke care especially, that window is everything.

I know what I don't have on paper: a title that says I've sold directly into a hospital or health system. What I do have is proof of the underlying work that title is meant to demonstrate. At Goldman, I managed complex institutional accounts where getting to yes meant aligning finance, legal, and operations stakeholders around a single outcome, not unlike building consensus across a P&T committee. At Vivint, I built and presented the executive forecasting and competitive analysis that won a $2M+ business case directly to C-suite leadership. And as a full-time volunteer representative running my own three-state territory, I built it from underperforming to one of the strongest in the region through daily pre-call planning, tracked outreach, and consistently hitting hard weekly targets, with zero formal sales title attached to any of it.

I'm also clinically grounded in a way most candidates coming from a traditional sales background aren't. I've stood in the emergency department during high-acuity care, I've met the credentialing and safety standards a hospital system requires of anyone inside it, and I can hold a real conversation about disease state and patient impact from day one. And I'm bilingual in Spanish, which across DFW health systems means genuine rapport with the staff who often decide how much time a physician has for you.

I live in the DFW metro, my kids are in preschool with full-time childcare in place, and I'm ready to build a territory around this launch. My approach is simple: know the science, know the stakeholders in the room, build the relationships that hold up under a real decision cycle, and keep pushing until the right information reaches the right person in time to matter.

startStories.title: Navigating Multi-Stakeholder Decisions
startStories.teaser: What it takes to get a room full of different priorities to yes.
startStories.body: At Goldman Sachs, a senior client pushed back on a contract term over a genuine misunderstanding. Getting that account back on track meant finding the misread myself, then aligning internal leadership, legal, and the client's own team around one resolution before it became a lost relationship. No single person in that decision had the full picture, and no single conversation would have fixed it. That is the same work of building consensus across a group with different priorities and different definitions of risk, whether the room is a finance committee or a hospital's own decision structure.

startStories.title: Winning at the C-Suite Level
startStories.teaser: Building the case, then defending it in the room.
startStories.body: At Vivint, I wasn't in the field. I was building the executive forecasting models and competitive market analysis that told the field where the opportunity actually was. I took that analysis directly to C-suite leadership and secured a $2M+ revenue expansion opportunity, defending the numbers in the room, not just handing over a slide deck. Institutional selling lives or dies on whether the person across the table trusts your data as much as they trust you.

startStories.title: Building a Territory With No Playbook
startStories.teaser: Eighteen months, three states, and a CRM pipeline I built myself.
startStories.body: As a full-time volunteer representative across Nebraska, Iowa, and South Dakota, I ran a three-state territory with no formal sales title attached to it. Every visit started with a written pre-call objective. Every visit ended with a post-call evaluation, tracked through my own CRM pipeline, so I could handle the next objection better than the last one. That discipline turned an underperforming territory into one of the strongest in the region, and it is the same discipline a launch territory needs from day one.

startStories.title: Earning Access Inside the Hospital System
startStories.teaser: Meeting the credentialing bar, then earning the trust that comes after it.
startStories.body: My EMT training put me inside an actual hospital system: the emergency department, patient transfers, and ambulance care, working alongside ER physicians, nurses, and trauma teams under full credentialing and safety compliance standards. Assisting during a high-acuity emergency procedure taught me to stay composed and useful under real pressure, inside the exact kind of environment where a rep has to earn the right to be in the room, not just show up with a badge.

startStories.title: Earning the Hardest Gatekeeper
startStories.teaser: The one contact everyone told me not to bother with.
startStories.body: One community leader I needed access through hadn't engaged with anyone from our group in years, and everyone before me said not to bother. Instead of pushing directly, I built a relationship with his wife first, learned he missed playing soccer with a group he'd lost touch with, and organized a recurring game and told him all he had to do was show up. He did, and over time he went from ignoring us completely to opening his entire network to us. Resistance is usually just information about what someone actually values, and that applies as much to a Head of Pharmacy as it does to a skeptical gatekeeper.

startStories.title: Reading the Competitive Landscape
startStories.teaser: Turning raw market data into a plan the field can actually use.
startStories.body: At 1-800 Contacts, I built a nationwide competitive and market analysis across 42,000+ U.S. ZIP codes to identify where spend and coverage should be concentrated, then personally trained the Analytic Team on how to use it. At Vivint, I took that same instinct further, diagnosing territory-level performance gaps with SQL, Snowflake, and Python and turning them into forecasting models leadership could act on. That is the analytical rigor behind a territory business plan: know the landscape before you walk in the door.
